title: Looped transformers: reusing depth, and what a second pass buys
summary: What it means to run the same layers more than once: depth versus parameters, the lineage from Adaptive Computation Time and the Universal Transformer through ALBERT, how Huginn's recurrent block works and why a trained loop count becomes a dial, the evidence that looping helps reasoning but not memorization (Saunshi et al., Ouro), SMELT's compute-matched test, the compute and cache bill, and why extra loops break models not trained for them. Hooked to an unverified screenshot claiming GPT-6.1 Sol uses two passes, and Pachocki's 'within a factor of two of GPT-4'.

topics: deep dive: looped transformers: reusing depth
concepts_taught: looped transformers as decoupling parameters (storage) from serial depth (steps): a k-layer block looped L times, with the lineage from Adaptive Computation Time (2016) and the Universal Transformer (2018, tied weights plus per-position halting) through ALBERT's cross-layer sharing, which saved storage but not arithmetic

the recurrent-depth recipe (Huginn): prelude, looped recurrent block, coda; random initial state with the input re-injected every pass; loop count sampled during training with truncated backprop, which is what turns loop count into a test-time dial, plus zero-shot per-token early exit

evidence and bill for looping: helps reasoning/knowledge manipulation but not memorization (~2 bits per parameter either way), only a modest gain once FLOPs, parameters and KV cache are matched (SMELT, 6.8-18% training compute), no saving in arithmetic or per-pass KV cache, and extrapolating past an untrained loop count degrades or collapses the model
